chunks: And from him (Al-Hilli) from Safwan ibn Yahya, who said: I said to Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Musa (peace be upon him):

Ibn al-Sarrag narrated from you that he asked you about a man who enters into Ihram for Hajj, then enters Mecca, performs Tawaf around the House seven times, and Sa'i between Safa and Marwah, then breaks that (Ihram) and makes it Umrah (Mut'ah). You said to him, 'No.' He said, 'I asked him about that, so I said to him, No, and he may release himself and make it Umrah.' And the last time my father met Al-Fadl ibn al-Rabii', he was wearing two woolen garments and silk (or silk-lined). Al-Fadl ibn al-Rabii' said to him, 'O Abu al-Hasan, we take you as a role model: you are performing Hajj al-Tamattu' (or rather, you are Mufrid?), and I am Mufrid.' My father said to him, 'No, I am not Mufrid; I am Mutamatti'. He said to him, 'Then I should now perform Mut'ah, and I have already Tawafed around the House.' My father said to him, 'Yes.' Muhammad ibn Ja'far took this to Sufyan ibn Uyaynah and his companions and said to them, 'Indeed, Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both) said such and such to Al-Fadl ibn al-Rabii', using it to criticize my father.'

And the Mufrid (one performing Hajj al-Mufrad) who enters Ihram after Tawaf and Sa'i, before shortening (his hair/nails), has no Mut'ah; he remains in his Ihram, and his Hajj is Mufrad. He narrated that.

key_terms.ثَوْبَانِ وَ سَاجٌ: Two woolen garments and silk (indicative of Ihram or specific dress)
key_terms.مُتَمَتِّعٌ: One performing Hajj al-Tamattu' (combined Umrah and Hajj)
key_terms.يُبْقَى عَلَى إِحْرَامِهِ: Remains in his state of Ihram

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Hajj al-Mufrad and Hajj al-Tamattu' according to Imam al-Rida (AS)?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the jurisprudential nuance between Hajj al-Mufrad and Hajj al-Tamattu' through Imam al-Rida’s (AS) clarification with Al-Fadl ibn al-Rabii', illustrating how early Shia scholars engaged with contemporary jurists like Sufyan ibn Uyayna. It establishes that performing Umrah rites before the Hajr season allows for a valid transition to Tamattu', while the Mufrid remains bound to his initial intention until the final sacrifice. This narrative underscores the dynamic nature of Shia fiqh in reconciling ritual actions with specific temporal conditions.
